# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review: Varga & Holm, comment on the Halden pilot

The comment does two different things, and they deserve different verdicts.

- **Sections 1–4 are a careful, valuable re-analysis.** They show the published pilot overstated its result, and several findings would warrant a correction to the working paper.
- **Sections 6–8 and the headline conclusion go well beyond that evidence.** The claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is not established, and it is contradicted by the randomised trial the comment itself cites.

## Arithmetic checks

Most figures reproduce:

| Item | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Table 2, rows 1–4 | 98.7/0.8; 95.1/0.8; 98.4/0.859; 95.4/0.861 | +23.4%, +18.9%, +14.6%, +10.8% ✓ |
| Hours ratios | 34.6/40.3 = 0.859; 34.8/40.4 = 0.861 | ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014/1.041 − 1 | −2.6% ✓ |
| 19 of 23 managers above records | sign test | p ≈ 0.003 two-sided, so the bias is clearly systematic |

Three figures do not reproduce:

- **The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Baseline actual hours were 40.3, about 8.06 per day. Adding 0.7 h/day over four days and 1.6 h on the day off gives roughly 4 × 8.76 + 1.6 ≈ 36.6 hours, not 34.6. Either the +0.7 is measured against a different base, or one of the figures is wrong. Since the denominator correction is central to the comment, this needs reconciling.
- **The exit reasons don't sum to nine.** Six withdrawals cited workload and two cited scheduling, which is eight of nine. What did the ninth give?
- **The novelty extrapolation is off by a month.** Energy fell 0.32 SD between months 3 and 6, about 0.107 per month. Extrapolating linearly, it reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." This is minor, but see §4 on the extrapolation itself.

## 1. Strong contributions

- **Attrition (§1).** This is the most important finding. The working paper says withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show seven of nine left *after* the schedule began, mostly citing workload. That is a substantive misstatement in the original paper, not a matter of interpretation.
- **Manager index versus records (§2).** This is a direct, well-designed test of the bias I flagged in my review of the working paper. It is also generously framed.
- **Hours and revenue (§§3–4).** These are sensible, documented corrections.
- **Data note.** It honestly states that the corrections apply only to subsets.

## 2. The abstract and conclusion misstate what was done

- **Attrition is not actually corrected.** The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems brings the gain to 10.8%, and the first problem is attrition. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is documented but never quantified. Seven organisations withdrew after starting, so the microdata probably contain one or two months of output index for them. The authors could then:
  - run an intention-to-treat analysis on all 70 organisations;
  - or report bounds on the effect, such as Lee bounds or worst-case imputation.

  Without that, the attrition effect is an assertion, however plausible.
- **Revenue cannot explain any of the per-hour gain.** The 23.4% never uses revenue. Listing revenue among four problems that "account for most of the reported gain" is incorrect, even though the revenue point stands on its own.
- **The abstract contradicts itself.** It says the problems "account for most" of the gain, and two sentences later that the gain is "entirely an artifact."

## 3. Table 2 mixes different samples

Each row uses a different set of organisations: 61, 23, 27 and 17. The drops between rows therefore mix the effect of each correction with differences between samples. The progression is not a clean decomposition. It would be much clearer to show all four specifications on the same 17 organisations, starting from their as-reported figure.

There are also no confidence intervals anywhere. With 17 organisations, the 10.8% has substantial uncertainty, and so do the comparisons between rows.

One further check is needed on the output measure itself. Some record-based measures are "billable hours delivered." Under a reduced-hours scheme, billable hours fall almost mechanically with time worked, so this would bias the record-based index *downward*. The authors should say how many of the 23 organisations used that measure, and show the comparison with them excluded.

## 4. The novelty argument rests on indirect evidence

- **Energy is not output.** The argument infers the trajectory of output from the trajectory of self-reported energy.
- **The microdata can test this directly.** Halden collected the output index *monthly*, so the authors can simply test whether output per hour declines across months one to six. That direct test should replace the indirect one.
- **The extrapolation is fragile.** It draws a straight line through two points and projects beyond the observed data. Energy could just as easily level off above zero.
- **The burden-of-proof argument works against the conclusion.** It supports saying durability is *unproven*. It does not support concluding the effect is *zero*. The comment moves from the first to the second.

## 5. The comment omits the main positive result of the trial it cites

This is the most serious problem.

The comment treats the Varden counter-stratum result as "the most reliable finding in the literature." The same trial's case-processing stratum used every safeguard the comment recommends:
- record-based output;
- actual hours from timesheets;
- a randomised control group, which addresses selection;
- nine months' duration, longer than Halden's six;
- no attrition at the office level.

It found output per actual hour **+12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**. That is strikingly close to the comment's own corrected 10.8%.

Novelty is the only explanation not addressed by that design. So the strongest conclusion the evidence supports is roughly this:

> Corrected estimates of the per-hour gain are around 10–13% in work not tied to presence, and that is consistent across a pilot and a randomised trial. Whether the gain lasts remains open.

That is a meaningful downward correction of Halden's 23.4%. It is not "entirely an artifact."

## 6. The treatment of the meetings analysis is inaccurate

- **Not post hoc.** The meeting data were collected in month six, during the trial and before the nine-month results existed.
- **Not a subgroup.** The seven offices are the entire treated arm of a pre-specified stratum, not a selected subgroup.
- **Varden already says this.** Varden explicitly calls the analysis unregistered, states that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test. Telling readers it "should not be cited as a mechanism" repeats Varden's own caveat as if it were a rebuttal.
- **Uneven standards.** The comment dismisses n = 7 here while relying on n = 3 for the retail figure (−11.2%) and on two data points for the novelty projection.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Is the Varden comparison like for like?** Comparing Halden retail (−11.2%, three organisations) with Varden's counter stratum (−11.4% per FTE) is suggestive, but private retail and public counter services differ. The parallel shows consistent direction, not confirmation.
- **The conclusion is wider than the data.** "Per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" generalises from one pilot to the whole literature, which contradicts the data note's own caution.
- **Real revenue.** Deflating by CPI is reasonable. Still, a real fall of 2.6% without a counterfactual doesn't show the pilot caused it, just as the nominal rise didn't show the opposite.

## Overall

Sections 1–4 should be published largely as they are, with the hours arithmetic reconciled and a same-subset version of Table 2. Together they make a convincing case that Halden's 23.4% is roughly half overstatement.

The conclusion should be rewritten to match what the evidence shows:
- corrected gains of about 11% in this pilot, consistent with Varden's randomised 12.5%;
- clear losses in coverage-bound work;
- durability not yet established.

The recommendations for future evaluations are good, and Varden already meets most of them.

I can draft a referee report in journal format, or a short synthesis of where the three documents now leave the evidence, if either would be useful.
